items.prompt: Minute 1: the interviewer says 'Design a food-delivery app.' You don't yet know which features or what scale matter.
items.why: Nothing is scoped yet → step 1 of the framework: clarify functional and non-functional requirements before numbers or APIs.

items.prompt: Scope is agreed: 20 M daily users, each places 2 orders a week, order history kept 3 years. What do you do next?
items.why: You now have raw numbers → turn them into QPS and storage before choosing any building block.

items.prompt: Your v1 diagram is client → service → database, and your estimate says 40 000 reads/s of the same restaurant menus with rare edits.
items.why: Read-heavy, repeated, rarely changing data → v2 adds a cache on the read path (the read-heavy smell).

items.prompt: When an order is placed, the restaurant, the courier matcher and the email service must all react, and the user shouldn't wait for any of them.
items.why: Fan-out to several consumers off the request path → publish an 'order placed' event to a queue or log.

items.prompt: You're defining how the mobile app creates an order and lists past orders, including pagination and safe retries.
items.why: Endpoints, pagination and idempotent retries are API design, part of the high-level step.

items.prompt: In the wrap-up the interviewer asks what happens if the region hosting the primary database goes down.
items.why: Surviving the loss of a whole region's database is a failure-mode question → replicas in another region and a failover plan.

items.prompt: Ten minutes in, you've drawn twelve boxes including a search cluster and a stream processor, but you haven't written down any requirement.
items.why: Boxes not justified by requirements or numbers is a process problem → go back to scope and evolve from a simple v1.

items.prompt: Partners call the public order-status API in tight loops and are degrading the service for everyone.
items.why: A noisy client harming others → per-key quotas with 429 responses (a rate limiter at the gateway).
